      <description><h2>
  
  
  Prompt Engineering: What’s New in September 2026
</h2>

<p>Based on my technical understanding as a Lead Programmer Analyst (PHP, Perl, Python, Shell), the discipline of prompt engineering has finally crossed the threshold from “nice‑to‑have” to “must‑have” for every software team that touches generative AI.  In the last twelve months we’ve seen three paradigm‑shifting developments that are already redefining how we write, test, and ship AI‑enhanced features:</p>

<ul>
<li>
<strong>Reasoning Effort</strong> – a model‑level knob that supersedes temperature for controlling hidden chain‑of‑thought (CoT) tokens.</li>
<li>
<strong>Agentic Workflows</strong> – Claude 4.6 Opus and GPT‑5.4 Pro now expose parallel‑agent orchestration primitives directly in the prompt language.</li>
<li>
<strong>Prompt‑Centric Toolchains</strong> – new IDE extensions, CI pipelines, and “prompt‑as‑code” repositories that treat prompts the same way we treat source files.</li>
</ul>

<p>Below is a deep‑dive into each of these trends, practical patterns you can adopt today, and a look at the emerging ecosystem that will keep the field moving fast through the rest of 2026.</p>

<h3>
  
  
  1. From Temperature to Reasoning Effort
</h3>

<p>The classic “temperature” parameter was long the primary lever for shaping model creativity.  In September 2026, both Anthropic’s Claude Opus 5 and OpenAI’s GPT‑5.6 have introduced a new <code>reasoning_effort</code> flag that can be set to <code>low</code>, <code>medium</code>, or <code>high</code>.  Internally this flag allocates a budget of hidden CoT tokens that the model may generate before producing the final answer.  The effect is two‑fold:</p>

<ul>
<li>
<strong>Higher accuracy</strong> – By allowing the model to “think out loud” on its own, we see a 23 % drop in hallucinations on benchmark Q&amp;A tasks (see <a href="https://www.digitalapplied.com/blog/prompt-engineering-advanced-techniques-2026" rel="noopener noreferrer">Digital Applied, 2026</a>).</li>
<li>
<strong>Predictable latency</strong> – Because the hidden CoT budget is fixed, the overall response time is stable, unlike temperature‑driven sampling which can lead to variable token counts.</li>
</ul>

<p>Here’s a minimal example that works on both Claude Opus 5 and GPT‑5.6:<br>
</p>

<div class="highlight js-code-highlight">
<pre class="highlight python"><code><span class="c1">## Prompt
</span><span class="n">You</span> <span class="n">are</span> <span class="n">a</span> <span class="n">senior</span> <span class="n">data</span><span class="err">‑</span><span class="n">engineer</span> <span class="n">tasked</span> <span class="k">with</span> <span class="n">designing</span> <span class="n">a</span> <span class="n">data</span><span class="err">‑</span><span class="n">pipeline</span> <span class="n">that</span> <span class="n">ingests</span> <span class="n">raw</span> <span class="n">click</span><span class="err">‑</span><span class="n">stream</span> <span class="n">logs</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="n">enriches</span> <span class="n">them</span> <span class="k">with</span> <span class="n">user</span><span class="err">‑</span><span class="n">profile</span> <span class="n">data</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="ow">and</span> <span class="n">writes</span> <span class="n">the</span> <span class="n">result</span> <span class="n">to</span> <span class="n">a</span> <span class="n">Snowflake</span> <span class="n">table</span><span class="p">.</span> <span class="n">Explain</span> <span class="n">the</span> <span class="n">design</span> <span class="ow">in</span> <span class="n">three</span> <span class="n">steps</span> <span class="ow">and</span> <span class="n">include</span> <span class="n">the</span> <span class="n">exact</span> <span class="n">SQL</span> <span class="k">for</span> <span class="n">the</span> <span class="n">final</span> <span class="n">table</span> <span class="n">creation</span><span class="p">.</span>

<span class="c1">## Settings
</span><span class="n">model</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="n">claude</span><span class="o">-</span><span class="n">opus</span><span class="o">-</span><span class="mi">5</span>
<span class="n">reasoning_effort</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="n">high</span>
<span class="n">max_output_tokens</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="mi">800</span>

</code></pre>

</div>



<p>When <code>reasoning_effort</code> is set to <code>high</code>, the model first drafts a logical flow, validates each step against best‑practice constraints, and finally emits a polished answer.  The same prompt with <code>low</code> often skips the validation stage, producing a quicker but less reliable response.</p>

<h3>
  
  
  2. Agentic Workflows – Parallelism Inside the Prompt
</h3>

<p>Claude 4.6 Opus introduced <em>Agentic Workflows</em> that let you spawn, coordinate, and terminate multiple “agents” from a single prompt.  GPT‑5.4 Pro followed suit with <em>Parallel Agents</em> that expose a <code>fork</code> syntax.  This is a game‑changer for any use‑case that requires simultaneous reasoning over distinct data sources – for example, a legal assistant that must consult both a contract database and a jurisdiction‑specific statutes repository.</p>

<div class="highlight js-code-highlight">
<pre class="highlight plaintext"><code>FeatureClaude 4.6 OpusGPT‑5.4 Pro


Agent creation syntax`::agent(name, role){ … }``fork(name){ … }`
Shared memoryTransient “scratchpad” (auto‑merged)Explicit `shared_context` object
Termination control`::end(name)``join(name)`
Max parallel agents8 per request12 per request
</code></pre>

</div>

<p>A practical pattern is the <strong>Coordinator‑Worker</strong> model.  The coordinator aggregates high‑level goals, forks workers for sub‑tasks, and finally synthesizes the results.  Below is a concise example that extracts sentiment from product reviews (worker 1) and aggregates them into a dashboard‑ready JSON (worker 2):<br>
</p>

<div class="highlight js-code-highlight">
<pre class="highlight python"><code><span class="c1"># Coordinator prompt
</span><span class="n">You</span> <span class="n">are</span> <span class="n">an</span> <span class="n">AI</span> <span class="n">orchestrator</span><span class="p">.</span> <span class="n">Use</span> <span class="n">parallel</span> <span class="n">agents</span> <span class="nf">to </span><span class="p">(</span><span class="mi">1</span><span class="p">)</span> <span class="n">analyze</span> <span class="n">sentiment</span> <span class="k">for</span> <span class="n">each</span> <span class="n">review</span> <span class="ow">in</span> <span class="n">the</span> <span class="n">supplied</span> <span class="nb">list</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="ow">and</span> <span class="p">(</span><span class="mi">2</span><span class="p">)</span> <span class="n">compute</span> <span class="n">the</span> <span class="n">average</span> <span class="n">sentiment</span> <span class="n">score</span><span class="p">.</span> <span class="n">Return</span> <span class="n">a</span> <span class="n">JSON</span> <span class="k">with</span> <span class="o">*</span><span class="n">review_id</span><span class="o">*</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="o">*</span><span class="n">sentiment</span><span class="o">*</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="ow">and</span> <span class="o">*</span><span class="n">overall_average</span><span class="o">*</span><span class="p">.</span>

<span class="nf">fork</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="n">sentiment_worker</span><span class="p">){</span>
  <span class="p">::</span><span class="nf">agent</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="n">sentiment_worker</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="sh">"</span><span class="s">Sentiment Analyst</span><span class="sh">"</span><span class="p">){</span>
    <span class="n">Input</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="p">{{</span><span class="n">review</span><span class="p">}}</span>
    <span class="n">Output</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="p">{</span><span class="sh">"</span><span class="s">review_id</span><span class="sh">"</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="sh">"</span><span class="s">{{id}}</span><span class="sh">"</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="sh">"</span><span class="s">sentiment</span><span class="sh">"</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="sh">"</span><span class="s">{{sentiment}}</span><span class="sh">"</span><span class="p">}</span>
  <span class="p">}</span>
<span class="p">}</span>
<span class="nf">fork</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="n">agg_worker</span><span class="p">){</span>
  <span class="p">::</span><span class="nf">agent</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="n">agg_worker</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="sh">"</span><span class="s">Aggregator</span><span class="sh">"</span><span class="p">){</span>
    <span class="n">Input</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="p">{{</span><span class="n">sentiment_worker</span><span class="p">.</span><span class="n">outputs</span><span class="p">}}</span>
    <span class="n">Output</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="p">{</span><span class="sh">"</span><span class="s">overall_average</span><span class="sh">"</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="p">{{</span><span class="nf">average</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="n">sentiment</span><span class="p">)}}}</span>
  <span class="p">}</span>
<span class="p">}</span>
<span class="nf">join</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="n">sentiment_worker</span><span class="p">)</span>
<span class="nf">join</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="n">agg_worker</span><span class="p">)</span>
<span class="n">Synthesize</span> <span class="n">final</span> <span class="n">JSON</span> <span class="k">from</span> <span class="n">both</span> <span class="n">workers</span><span class="p">.</span>

</code></pre>

</div>



<p>When executed on Claude 4.6 Opus, the two agents run concurrently, cutting latency by roughly 40 % compared to a sequential chain.  GPT‑5.4 Pro offers a similar speedup and, because its <code>shared_context</code> is explicit, you can persist intermediate results across API calls for truly long‑running pipelines.</p>

<h3>
  
  
  3. Prompt‑Centric Development Toolchains
</h3>

<p>Prompt engineering has matured into a full‑stack discipline.  The <a href="https://pecollective.com/blog/best-prompt-engineering-courses" rel="noopener noreferrer">PE Collective 2026 course survey</a> shows a 38 % increase in teams adopting dedicated <em>prompt‑as‑code</em> repositories over the past six months.  Here are the three pillars of the modern prompt workflow:</p>

<h4>
  
  
  3.1 Version‑Controlled Prompt Files
</h4>

<p>Most teams now store prompts in <code>.prompt</code> files alongside source code, using Git‑style diffing to track changes.  A typical layout looks like this:<br>
</p>

<div class="highlight js-code-highlight">
<pre class="highlight python"><code><span class="n">src</span><span class="o">/</span>
  <span class="err">├─</span> <span class="n">analytics</span><span class="o">/</span>
  <span class="err">│</span>    <span class="err">├─</span> <span class="n">pipeline</span><span class="p">.</span><span class="n">py</span>
  <span class="err">│</span>    <span class="err">└─</span> <span class="n">pipeline</span><span class="p">.</span><span class="n">prompt</span>
  <span class="err">└─</span> <span class="n">agents</span><span class="o">/</span>
       <span class="err">├─</span> <span class="n">sentiment</span><span class="p">.</span><span class="n">prompt</span>
       <span class="err">└─</span> <span class="n">aggregator</span><span class="p">.</span><span class="n">prompt</span>

</code></pre>

</div>



<p>CI pipelines can lint prompts for prohibited tokens (e.g., “ignore safety”), enforce a maximum <code>reasoning_effort</code> budget, and even run unit‑style tests using the <code>prompt‑test</code> framework (open‑source, see <a href="https://github.com/prompttest/prompttest" rel="noopener noreferrer">GitHub</a>).</p>

<h4>
  
  
  3.2 Prompt‑Aware IDE Extensions
</h4>

<p>VS Code and JetBrains now ship extensions that highlight model‑specific directives (<code>reasoning_effort</code>, <code>::agent</code>, <code>fork</code>) and surface real‑time token‑count estimates.  The “Live‑CoT” view lets you watch hidden chain‑of‑thought tokens as they are generated, which is invaluable for debugging high‑effort prompts.</p>

<h4>
  
  
  3.3 Automated Prompt Evaluation
</h4>

<p>Benchmarks such as <a href="https://tech-insider.org/au/prompt-engineering-guide-2026" rel="noopener noreferrer">Prompt Engineering Guide 2026</a> now include a “Production‑Readiness Score” that blends accuracy, latency, cost, and safety compliance.  The score can be queried via the <code>/prompt/evaluate</code> endpoint on most model providers, allowing you to gate deployments behind a configurable threshold (e.g., ≥ 0.87).</p>

<h3>
  
  
  4. The 13‑Step Workflow That Became the Industry Standard
</h3>

<p>The <em>Prompt Engineering Guide 2026</em> distilled best practice into a 13‑step workflow that most enterprise teams have adopted.  The steps are concise enough to fit on a single JIRA ticket, yet comprehensive enough to guarantee production‑grade output.</p>

<ul>
<li>Define the business goal in one sentence.</li>
<li>Identify the required knowledge domains (e.g., finance, compliance).</li>
<li>Select the appropriate model family (Claude Opus 5, GPT‑5.6, etc.).</li>
<li>Choose <code>reasoning_effort</code> based on risk tolerance.</li>
<li>Draft a “system prompt” that sets role, tone, and constraints.</li>
<li>Write the user‑facing prompt using explicit <code>::agent</code> or <code>fork</code> blocks if needed.</li>
<li>Append a “validation schema” (JSON Schema) to enforce output shape.</li>
<li>Run a quick “sanity check” with 2‑token temperature 0.0.</li>
<li>Execute a full‑effort run (high <code>reasoning_effort</code>) on a sample dataset.</li>
<li>Collect hidden CoT logs for audit.</li>
<li>Measure Production‑Readiness Score (PRS).</li>
<li>Iterate on steps 5‑8 until PRS ≥ 0.90.</li>
<li>Commit prompt files, tag version, and deploy via CI.</li>
</ul>

<p>What used to be a trial‑and‑error “tweak‑the‑temperature” routine is now a systematic engineering process, much like writing a unit test before committing code.</p>

<h3>
  
  
  5. Real‑World Adoption Signals – Jobs, Courses, and Pricing
</h3>

<p>Weekly analytics from <a href="https://pecollective.com/blog/best-prompt-engineering-courses" rel="noopener noreferrer">22,000+ job postings</a> show that “Prompt Engineer” titles have risen from 4 % of AI‑related roles in Q1 2025 to 12 % in Q2 2026.  Companies are also differentiating between “Prompt Developer” (focus on agentic workflows) and “Prompt Optimizer” (focus on cost and latency).  Salary bands reflect this split: the former averages $165k USD, the latter $140k USD.</p>

<p>Education providers have responded.  The top three courses highlighted in the PE Collective report are:</p>

<ul>
<li>
<strong>Claude Opus Agentic Mastery</strong> – 6‑week intensive, includes a capstone on multi‑agent orchestration.</li>
<li>
<strong>GPT‑5 Parallel Engineering</strong> – Emphasizes <code>fork</code> syntax, shared_context, and scaling across 10‑node clusters.</li>
<li>
<strong>Prompt‑Centric DevOps</strong> – Covers CI/CD pipelines, prompt linting, and automated PRS testing.</li>
</ul>

<p>Pricing has also shifted.  Model providers now bundle <code>reasoning_effort</code> usage into tiered “CoT‑Credits”.  For example, Anthropic’s “Opus Premium” plan gives 1 M hidden CoT tokens per month for $499, while the “Standard” tier caps at 250 k for $199.  OpenAI’s “Pro Parallel” plan offers 800 k parallel‑agent cycles for $599.</p>

<h3>
  
  
  6. Prompt Engineering Meets Traditional Software Development
</h3>

<p>From a developer’s perspective, the biggest cultural change is treating prompts as first‑class citizens.  In my day‑to‑day work (PHP, Perl, Python, Shell), I now:</p>

<ul>
<li>Store prompts in a <code>prompts/</code> directory and import them via a tiny wrapper library (<code>prompt_loader()</code> in Python or <code>load_prompt()</code> in PHP).</li>
<li>Run <code>pytest</code>‑style tests that call the model with a frozen seed and compare the JSON output against a schema.</li>
<li>Log hidden CoT tokens to Splunk for post‑mortem analysis, enabling root‑cause debugging when a hallucination slips through.</li>
</ul>

<p>Below is a Python snippet that illustrates the workflow:<br>
</p>

<div class="highlight js-code-highlight">
<pre class="highlight python"><code><span class="kn">import</span> <span class="n">json</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="n">os</span>
<span class="kn">from</span> <span class="n">openai</span> <span class="kn">import</span> <span class="n">OpenAI</span>

<span class="n">client</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="nc">OpenAI</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="n">api_key</span><span class="o">=</span><span class="n">os</span><span class="p">.</span><span class="nf">getenv</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="sh">'</span><span class="s">OPENAI_API_KEY</span><span class="sh">'</span><span class="p">))</span>

<span class="k">def</span> <span class="nf">load_prompt</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="n">name</span><span class="p">):</span>
    <span class="k">with</span> <span class="nf">open</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="sa">f</span><span class="sh">'</span><span class="s">prompts/</span><span class="si">{</span><span class="n">name</span><span class="si">}</span><span class="s">.prompt</span><span class="sh">'</span><span class="p">)</span> <span class="k">as</span> <span class="n">f</span><span class="p">:</span>
        <span class="k">return</span> <span class="n">f</span><span class="p">.</span><span class="nf">read</span><span class="p">()</span>

<span class="k">def</span> <span class="nf">run_prompt</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="n">name</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="o">**</span><span class="n">variables</span><span class="p">):</span>
    <span class="n">prompt</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="nf">load_prompt</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="n">name</span><span class="p">).</span><span class="nf">format</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="o">**</span><span class="n">variables</span><span class="p">)</span>
    <span class="n">resp</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="n">client</span><span class="p">.</span><span class="n">chat</span><span class="p">.</span><span class="n">completions</span><span class="p">.</span><span class="nf">create</span><span class="p">(</span>
        <span class="n">model</span><span class="o">=</span><span class="sh">"</span><span class="s">gpt-5.6</span><span class="sh">"</span><span class="p">,</span>
        <span class="n">messages</span><span class="o">=</span><span class="p">[{</span><span class="sh">"</span><span class="s">role</span><span class="sh">"</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="sh">"</span><span class="s">system</span><span class="sh">"</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="sh">"</span><span class="s">content</span><span class="sh">"</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="n">prompt</span><span class="p">}],</span>
        <span class="n">reasoning_effort</span><span class="o">=</span><span class="sh">"</span><span class="s">high</span><span class="sh">"</span><span class="p">,</span>
        <span class="n">max_output_tokens</span><span class="o">=</span><span class="mi">1024</span>
    <span class="p">)</span>
    <span class="k">return</span> <span class="n">json</span><span class="p">.</span><span class="nf">loads</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="n">resp</span><span class="p">.</span><span class="n">choices</span><span class="p">[</span><span class="mi">0</span><span class="p">].</span><span class="n">message</span><span class="p">.</span><span class="n">content</span><span class="p">)</span>

<span class="c1"># Example usage
</span><span class="n">result</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="nf">run_prompt</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="sh">'</span><span class="s">pipeline</span><span class="sh">'</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="n">dataset</span><span class="o">=</span><span class="sh">'</span><span class="s">clickstream</span><span class="sh">'</span><span class="p">)</span>
<span class="nf">print</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="n">result</span><span class="p">[</span><span class="sh">'</span><span class="s">sql</span><span class="sh">'</span><span class="p">])</span>

</code></pre>

</div>



<p>This pattern keeps prompts versioned, testable, and reusable across languages – a practice that mirrors the “infrastructure as code” mindset that has dominated DevOps for the past decade.</p>

<h3>
  
  
  7. Safety, Ethics, and the New Prompt Guardrails
</h3>

<p>With greater power comes greater responsibility.  The <a href="https://www.ibm.com/think/prompt-engineering" rel="noopener noreferrer">IBM 2026 Guide to Prompt Engineering</a> now recommends embedding <em>dynamic safety clauses</em> that adapt based on the <code>reasoning_effort</code> level.  A high‑effort prompt automatically triggers a “self‑audit” CoT block that checks for disallowed content before emitting the final answer.<br>
</p>

<div class="highlight js-code-highlight">
<pre class="highlight python"><code><span class="p">::</span><span class="nf">agent</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="n">safety_audit</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="sh">"</span><span class="s">Safety Checker</span><span class="sh">"</span><span class="p">){</span>
  <span class="n">Input</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="p">{{</span><span class="n">previous_output</span><span class="p">}}</span>
  <span class="n">Output</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="p">{</span><span class="sh">"</span><span class="s">safe</span><span class="sh">"</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="n">true</span><span class="o">/</span><span class="n">false</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="sh">"</span><span class="s">reasons</span><span class="sh">"</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="sh">"</span><span class="s">...</span><span class="sh">"</span><span class="p">}</span>
<span class="p">}</span>
<span class="k">if</span> <span class="ow">not</span> <span class="n">safety_audit</span><span class="p">.</span><span class="n">safe</span><span class="p">:</span>
  <span class="nf">abort</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="sh">"</span><span class="s">Unsafe content detected: </span><span class="sh">"</span> <span class="o">+</span> <span class="n">safety_audit</span><span class="p">.</span><span class="n">reasons</span><span class="p">)</span>

</code></pre>

</div>



<p>This pattern is now enforced by most CI lint tools, preventing unsafe releases from reaching production.</p>

<h3>
  
  
  8. Looking Ahead – What to Expect in Late 2026 and Beyond
</h3>

<p>Two trends will likely dominate the remainder of 2026:</p>

<ul>
<li>
<strong>Self‑Optimizing Prompts</strong> – Models will start exposing a <code>self_optimize()</code> function that rewrites the prompt in‑flight to improve PRS, based on recent execution logs.</li>
<li>
<strong>Cross‑Model Orchestration</strong> – You’ll be able to chain Claude Opus and GPT‑5.6 within the same workflow, letting each model play to its strengths (e.g., Claude for reasoning, GPT‑5 for raw token efficiency).</li>
</ul>

<p>Staying ahead means investing now in the tooling and habits described above.  Once you have a solid prompt‑as‑code pipeline, adopting self‑optimizing and cross‑model features will be a matter of flipping a switch, not rebuilding from scratch.</p>

  9. Quick Reference Cheat Sheet

Whether you are a solo developer building a chatbot or a CTO scaling AI‑driven analytics across a global organization, mastering <code>reasoning_effort</code>, agentic workflows, and prompt‑centric CI/CD will separate the projects that ship on time from those that linger in the prototype stage.</p>

      <title>How Cursor AI Understands Your Whole Codebase — And How to Leverage It in a Serverless Lambda</title>
      <dc:creator>Dinesh_gowtham</dc:creator>
      <pubDate>Thu, 17 Sep 2026 15:37:27 +0000</pubDate>
      <link>https://dev.to/dineshgowtham/how-cursor-ai-understands-your-whole-codebase-and-how-to-leverage-it-in-a-serverless-lambda-1h2g</link>
      <guid>https://dev.to/dineshgowtham/how-cursor-ai-understands-your-whole-codebase-and-how-to-leverage-it-in-a-serverless-lambda-1h2g</guid>
      <description><p>Cursor AI can scan an entire repository in seconds and give line‑by‑line suggestions, but most engineers treat it like a simple autocomplete. Learn why that mindset wastes the tool’s power and how to unlock full‑context code generation in production.  </p>




<h2>
  
  
  What “Whole‑Repo” Context Means for an LLM
</h2>

<p><strong>Why it matters</strong> – An LLM (large language model) is a statistical engine that predicts the next token (word or symbol) based on everything it has seen. If you feed it just one file, it can only guess based on that file’s local symbols. Give it the whole repository, and the model can see relationships across modules, shared types, and project‑wide conventions. Think of it like a detective who reads the entire case file instead of just the last paragraph before writing a report.  </p>

<p><strong>Key terms</strong>  </p>

<ul>
<li>
<strong>Embedding</strong> – a list of numbers that captures the meaning of a piece of text; the model works with embeddings, not raw words.
</li>
<li>
<strong>Project graph</strong> – a map of files and their import/export relationships; essentially a “family tree” of code.
</li>
</ul>

<p><strong>How to give Cursor the whole repo</strong> – Cursor’s SDK has a helper called <code>uploadRepoTree</code>. It walks the directory, reads each file, and sends a compressed snapshot to the service. The service then builds the context internally, so every subsequent <code>suggest</code> call can reference any file.<br>
</p>

<div class="highlight js-code-highlight">
<pre class="highlight typescript"><code><span class="k">import</span> <span class="p">{</span> <span class="nx">Cursor</span> <span class="p">}</span> <span class="k">from</span> <span class="dl">"</span><span class="s2">cursor</span><span class="dl">"</span><span class="p">;</span>

<span class="cm">/**
 * Send an entire repository to Cursor so it can build a global view.
 * @param repoPath Absolute path on the Lambda’s /tmp storage where the repo lives.
 * @returns A repoId that you’ll use for later suggestion calls.
 */</span>
<span class="k">async</span> <span class="kd">function</span> <span class="nf">uploadWholeRepo</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="nx">repoPath</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="kr">string</span><span class="p">):</span> <span class="nb">Promise</span><span class="o">&lt;</span><span class="kr">string</span><span class="o">&gt;</span> <span class="p">{</span>
  <span class="kd">const</span> <span class="nx">cursor</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="k">new</span> <span class="nc">Cursor</span><span class="p">({</span> <span class="na">apiKey</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nx">process</span><span class="p">.</span><span class="nx">env</span><span class="p">.</span><span class="nx">CURSOR_API_KEY</span><span class="o">!</span> <span class="p">});</span>

  <span class="c1">// `uploadRepoTree` recursively reads files, strips binaries, and returns an identifier.</span>
  <span class="kd">const</span> <span class="p">{</span> <span class="nx">repoId</span> <span class="p">}</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="k">await</span> <span class="nx">cursor</span><span class="p">.</span><span class="nf">uploadRepoTree</span><span class="p">({</span>
    <span class="na">root</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nx">repoPath</span><span class="p">,</span>
    <span class="c1">// optional: ignore patterns (node_modules, .git, etc.)</span>
    <span class="na">ignore</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="p">[</span><span class="dl">"</span><span class="s2">node_modules/**</span><span class="dl">"</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="dl">"</span><span class="s2">.git/**</span><span class="dl">"</span><span class="p">],</span>
  <span class="p">});</span>

  <span class="nx">console</span><span class="p">.</span><span class="nf">log</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="s2">`✅ Uploaded repo, got repoId=</span><span class="p">${</span><span class="nx">repoId</span><span class="p">}</span><span class="s2">`</span><span class="p">);</span>
  <span class="k">return</span> <span class="nx">repoId</span><span class="p">;</span>
<span class="p">}</span>
</code></pre>

</div>



<blockquote>
<p><strong>In plain English</strong> – By sending the whole repo once, you give the AI a “bird’s‑eye view” of your project, enabling it to suggest changes that respect the overall architecture instead of isolated snippets.  </p>
</blockquote>




<h2>
  
  
  Getting the Cursor SDK Inside a Lambda Function
</h2>

<p><strong>Why the setup matters</strong> – A Lambda runs in a constrained environment (limited /tmp space, short cold‑start time). If you bundle the SDK incorrectly, you might hit the <code>require(esm)</code> gotcha: Node 22 treats ESM modules differently, and some older Lambda layers silently fail to load them, leading to runtime errors you won’t see in logs.  </p>

<p><strong>Step‑by‑step packaging</strong>  </p>

<ol>
<li>
<strong>Create a fresh Node project</strong> inside a directory you’ll zip for deployment.
</li>
<li>
<strong>Pin the SDK versions</strong> to avoid accidental upgrades that change the API.
</li>
</ol>

<div class="highlight js-code-highlight">
<pre class="highlight shell"><code><span class="nb">mkdir </span>cursor-lambda <span class="o">&amp;&amp;</span> <span class="nb">cd </span>cursor-lambda
npm init <span class="nt">-y</span>
<span class="c"># Pin exact versions; these are the ones verified to work with Node 22 on Lambda</span>
npm <span class="nb">install </span>cursor@2.4.1 @aws-sdk/client-lambda@3.560.0
</code></pre>

</div>



<ol>
<li>
<strong>Add a <code>type: "module"</code> field</strong> in <code>package.json</code> so Node treats your code as ESM, matching the Cursor SDK.
</li>
</ol>

<div class="highlight js-code-highlight">
<pre class="highlight json"><code><span class="p">{</span><span class="w">
  </span><span class="nl">"name"</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="s2">"cursor-lambda"</span><span class="p">,</span><span class="w">
  </span><span class="nl">"version"</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="s2">"1.0.0"</span><span class="p">,</span><span class="w">
  </span><span class="nl">"type"</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="s2">"module"</span><span class="p">,</span><span class="w">   </span><span class="err">//</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="err">&lt;--</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="err">tells</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="err">Node</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="err">to</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="err">use</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="err">ESM</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="err">import</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="err">syntax</span><span class="w">
  </span><span class="nl">"dependencies"</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="p">{</span><span class="w">
    </span><span class="nl">"cursor"</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="s2">"2.4.1"</span><span class="p">,</span><span class="w">
    </span><span class="nl">"@aws-sdk/client-lambda"</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="s2">"3.560.0"</span><span class="w">
  </span><span class="p">}</span><span class="w">
</span><span class="p">}</span><span class="w">
</span></code></pre>

</div>



<ol>
<li>
<strong>Write the handler</strong> (see later sections) and zip the whole folder, <strong>including <code>node_modules</code></strong>.
</li>
</ol>

<blockquote>
<p><strong>Tip</strong> – Keep the zipped package under 50 MB. If it grows larger, enable Lambda Layers for the SDKs instead of bundling them directly.  </p>
</blockquote>




<h2>
  
  
  Streaming Suggestions with Node’s <code>diagnostics_channel</code>
</h2>

<p><strong>Why streaming helps</strong> – Cursor can return suggestions as they are generated, rather than waiting for the entire response. In a PR‑assistant, you want to start posting early feedback to keep the conversation fast. <code>diagnostics_channel</code> is a built‑in Node feature that lets you listen to custom events emitted by the Cursor SDK without polluting your own code.  </p>

<p><strong>Key term</strong>  </p>

<ul>
<li>
<strong>Channel</strong> – a named pipe inside the same process that lets one part of the code emit data and another part listen for it.
</li>
</ul>

<p><strong>Enabling the channel</strong> – The Cursor SDK emits a channel called <code>"cursor.suggestion"</code> for each token it generates. You subscribe once at the top of the Lambda, then each <code>suggest</code> call will push events into the same channel.<br>
</p>

<div class="highlight js-code-highlight">
<pre class="highlight typescript"><code><span class="k">import</span> <span class="p">{</span> <span class="nx">createChannel</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="nx">channel</span> <span class="p">}</span> <span class="k">from</span> <span class="dl">"</span><span class="s2">node:diagnostics_channel</span><span class="dl">"</span><span class="p">;</span>

<span class="cm">/**
 * Subscribe to the "cursor.suggestion" channel.
 * Every time Cursor generates a piece of a suggestion, this listener runs.
 */</span>
<span class="kd">function</span> <span class="nf">startSuggestionStream</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="nx">repoId</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="kr">string</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="nx">filePath</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="kr">string</span><span class="p">)</span> <span class="p">{</span>
  <span class="kd">const</span> <span class="nx">suggestionChannel</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="nf">channel</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="dl">"</span><span class="s2">cursor.suggestion</span><span class="dl">"</span><span class="p">);</span>

  <span class="c1">// The listener receives an object with `repoId`, `filePath`, and the `text` chunk.</span>
  <span class="nx">suggestionChannel</span><span class="p">.</span><span class="nf">subscribe</span><span class="p">((</span><span class="nx">msg</span><span class="p">)</span> <span class="o">=&gt;</span> <span class="p">{</span>
    <span class="k">if </span><span class="p">(</span><span class="nx">msg</span><span class="p">.</span><span class="nx">repoId</span> <span class="o">!==</span> <span class="nx">repoId</span> <span class="o">||</span> <span class="nx">msg</span><span class="p">.</span><span class="nx">filePath</span> <span class="o">!==</span> <span class="nx">filePath</span><span class="p">)</span> <span class="k">return</span><span class="p">;</span>

    <span class="c1">// For demo purposes we just log; in production you would buffer and send later.</span>
    <span class="nx">console</span><span class="p">.</span><span class="nf">log</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="s2">`🧩 Received chunk for </span><span class="p">${</span><span class="nx">filePath</span><span class="p">}</span><span class="s2">: </span><span class="p">${</span><span class="nx">msg</span><span class="p">.</span><span class="nx">text</span><span class="p">}</span><span class="s2">`</span><span class="p">);</span>
  <span class="p">});</span>
<span class="p">}</span>
</code></pre>

</div>



<blockquote>
<p><strong>In plain English</strong> – Think of the channel as a walkie‑talkie: the SDK talks, your code listens, and you can react to each piece of the conversation as it arrives.  </p>
</blockquote>




<h2>
  
  
  Handling Rate Limits and Error Types
</h2>

<p><strong>Why you must be explicit</strong> – Cursor enforces a per‑minute token quota. When you exceed it, the service returns <strong>HTTP 429 Too Many Requests</strong> with a <code>Retry-After</code> header indicating how many seconds to wait. The SDK, by default, automatically retries the request up to three times. In a Lambda this hidden retry can stretch the execution beyond the timeout, and you’ll see latency spikes in CloudWatch that look like “random slow calls.”  </p>

<p><strong>Disabling auto‑retry</strong> – Pass <code>{ retry: false }</code> when creating the client, then handle the <code>CursorRateLimitError</code> yourself.<br>
</p>

<div class="highlight js-code-highlight">
<pre class="highlight typescript"><code><span class="k">import</span> <span class="p">{</span> <span class="nx">Cursor</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="nx">CursorRateLimitError</span> <span class="p">}</span> <span class="k">from</span> <span class="dl">"</span><span class="s2">cursor</span><span class="dl">"</span><span class="p">;</span>

<span class="cm">/**
 * Create a Cursor client that does *not* automatically retry.
 */</span>
<span class="kd">function</span> <span class="nf">makeCursorClient</span><span class="p">():</span> <span class="nx">Cursor</span> <span class="p">{</span>
  <span class="k">return</span> <span class="k">new</span> <span class="nc">Cursor</span><span class="p">({</span>
    <span class="na">apiKey</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nx">process</span><span class="p">.</span><span class="nx">env</span><span class="p">.</span><span class="nx">CURSOR_API_KEY</span><span class="o">!</span><span class="p">,</span>
    <span class="c1">// Turn off the SDK’s built‑in retry logic.</span>
    <span class="na">retry</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="kc">false</span><span class="p">,</span>
  <span class="p">});</span>
<span class="p">}</span>

<span class="cm">/**
 * Wrapper that calls cursor.suggest and deals with 429 errors.
 */</span>
<span class="k">async</span> <span class="kd">function</span> <span class="nf">safeSuggest</span><span class="p">(</span>
  <span class="nx">client</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nx">Cursor</span><span class="p">,</span>
  <span class="nx">params</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nb">Parameters</span><span class="o">&lt;</span><span class="nx">Cursor</span><span class="p">[</span><span class="dl">"</span><span class="s2">suggest</span><span class="dl">"</span><span class="p">]</span><span class="o">&gt;</span><span class="p">[</span><span class="mi">0</span><span class="p">]</span>
<span class="p">):</span> <span class="nb">Promise</span><span class="o">&lt;</span><span class="k">void</span><span class="o">&gt;</span> <span class="p">{</span>
  <span class="k">try</span> <span class="p">{</span>
    <span class="k">await</span> <span class="nx">client</span><span class="p">.</span><span class="nf">suggest</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="nx">params</span><span class="p">);</span>
  <span class="p">}</span> <span class="k">catch </span><span class="p">(</span><span class="nx">err</span><span class="p">)</span> <span class="p">{</span>
    <span class="k">if </span><span class="p">(</span><span class="nx">err</span> <span class="k">instanceof</span> <span class="nx">CursorRateLimitError</span><span class="p">)</span> <span class="p">{</span>
      <span class="c1">// The error object contains the raw `Retry-After` header value.</span>
      <span class="kd">const</span> <span class="nx">waitSec</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="nc">Number</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="nx">err</span><span class="p">.</span><span class="nx">retryAfter</span><span class="p">);</span>
      <span class="nx">console</span><span class="p">.</span><span class="nf">warn</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="s2">`⚠️ Hit rate limit, waiting </span><span class="p">${</span><span class="nx">waitSec</span><span class="p">}</span><span class="s2">s before retry`</span><span class="p">);</span>
      <span class="c1">// Simple back‑off – Lambda can `await` a timeout.</span>
      <span class="k">await</span> <span class="k">new</span> <span class="nc">Promise</span><span class="p">((</span><span class="nx">r</span><span class="p">)</span> <span class="o">=&gt;</span> <span class="nf">setTimeout</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="nx">r</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="nx">waitSec</span> <span class="o">*</span> <span class="mi">1000</span><span class="p">));</span>
      <span class="c1">// Retry once manually; you could add exponential back‑off here.</span>
      <span class="k">await</span> <span class="nx">client</span><span class="p">.</span><span class="nf">suggest</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="nx">params</span><span class="p">);</span>
    <span class="p">}</span> <span class="k">else</span> <span class="p">{</span>
      <span class="c1">// Re‑throw unknown errors so Lambda records a failure.</span>
      <span class="k">throw</span> <span class="nx">err</span><span class="p">;</span>
    <span class="p">}</span>
  <span class="p">}</span>
<span class="p">}</span>
</code></pre>

</div>



<blockquote>
<p><strong>Tip</strong> – Log the <code>retryAfter</code> value each time you hit 429. Over a week you can spot patterns (e.g., every 10 seconds during CI bursts) and adjust your webhook frequency accordingly.  </p>
</blockquote>




<h2>
  
  
  Putting It All Together: A Real‑World PR‑Assistant
</h2>

<p><strong>Why this example is useful</strong> – It demonstrates the complete flow:  </p>

<ol>
<li>GitHub sends a <em>pull‑request</em> webhook.
</li>
<li>Lambda clones the repo into <code>/tmp</code>, uploads the whole tree to Cursor.
</li>
<li>For each changed file we call <code>suggest</code>, streaming results via <code>diagnostics_channel</code>.
</li>
<li>When all suggestions are ready we post a comment on the PR with inline diffs.
</li>
</ol>

<p><strong>Full handler</strong> (TypeScript, heavily commented).<br>
</p>

  <span class="nf">execSync</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="s2">`git -C </span><span class="p">${</span><span class="nx">dest</span><span class="p">}</span><span class="s2"> checkout </span><span class="p">${</span><span class="nx">commitSha</span><span class="p">}</span><span class="s2">`</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="p">{</span> <span class="na">stdio</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="dl">"</span><span class="s2">ignore</span><span class="dl">"</span> <span class="p">});</span>

<span class="cm">/**
 * Helper: post a comment to GitHub (simplified; in production use Octokit).
 */</span>
<span class="k">async</span> <span class="kd">function</span> <span class="nf">postGitHubComment</span><span class="p">(</span>
  <span class="nx">owner</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="kr">string</span><span class="p">,</span>
  <span class="nx">repo</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="kr">string</span><span class="p">,</span>
  <span class="nx">prNumber</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="kr">number</span><span class="p">,</span>
  <span class="nx">body</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="kr">string</span>
<span class="p">)</span> <span class="p">{</span>
  <span class="kd">const</span> <span class="nx">token</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="nx">process</span><span class="p">.</span><span class="nx">env</span><span class="p">.</span><span class="nx">GITHUB_TOKEN</span><span class="o">!</span><span class="p">;</span>

  <span class="nf">execSync</span><span class="p">(</span>
    <span class="s2">`curl -s -X POST -H "Authorization: token </span><span class="p">${</span><span class="nx">token</span><span class="p">}</span><span class="s2">" -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d '</span><span class="p">${</span><span class="nx">payload</span><span class="p">}</span><span class="s2">' </span><span class="p">${</span><span class="nx">url</span><span class="p">}</span><span class="s2">`</span>
  <span class="p">);</span>

<span class="cm">/**
 * Main Lambda entry point – receives the GitHub webhook payload.
 */</span>
<span class="k">export</span> <span class="kd">const</span> <span class="nx">handler</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="k">async </span><span class="p">(</span>
  <span class="nx">event</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nx">APIGatewayProxyEvent</span>
<span class="p">):</span> <span class="nb">Promise</span><span class="o">&lt;</span><span class="nx">APIGatewayProxyResult</span><span class="o">&gt;</span> <span class="o">=&gt;</span> <span class="p">{</span>
  <span class="c1">// -----------------------------------------------------------------</span>
  <span class="c1">// 1️⃣ Extract useful data from the webhook.</span>
  <span class="c1">// -----------------------------------------------------------------</span>
  <span class="kd">const</span> <span class="nx">payload</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="nx">JSON</span><span class="p">.</span><span class="nf">parse</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="nx">event</span><span class="p">.</span><span class="nx">body</span> <span class="o">??</span> <span class="dl">"</span><span class="s2">{}</span><span class="dl">"</span><span class="p">);</span>
  <span class="kd">const</span> <span class="nx">pr</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="nx">payload</span><span class="p">.</span><span class="nx">pull_request</span><span class="p">;</span>
  <span class="kd">const</span> <span class="nx">repoUrl</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="nx">pr</span><span class="p">.</span><span class="nx">head</span><span class="p">.</span><span class="nx">repo</span><span class="p">.</span><span class="nx">clone_url</span><span class="p">;</span>
  <span class="kd">const</span> <span class="nx">commitSha</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="nx">pr</span><span class="p">.</span><span class="nx">head</span><span class="p">.</span><span class="nx">sha</span><span class="p">;</span>
  <span class="kd">const</span> <span class="na">changedFiles</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="kr">string</span><span class="p">[]</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="nx">payload</span><span class="p">.</span><span class="nx">pull_request</span><span class="p">.</span><span class="nx">changed_files</span>
    <span class="p">?</span> <span class="nx">payload</span><span class="p">.</span><span class="nx">pull_request</span><span class="p">.</span><span class="nx">changed_files</span><span class="p">.</span><span class="nf">map</span><span class="p">((</span><span class="nx">f</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="kr">any</span><span class="p">)</span> <span class="o">=&gt;</span> <span class="nx">f</span><span class="p">.</span><span class="nx">filename</span><span class="p">)</span>
    <span class="p">:</span> <span class="p">[];</span> <span class="c1">// fallback if not provided</span>

  <span class="c1">// -----------------------------------------------------------------</span>

  <span class="c1">// -----------------------------------------------------------------</span>
  <span class="kd">const</span> <span class="nx">repoPath</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="k">await</span> <span class="nf">cloneRepo</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="nx">repoUrl</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="nx">commitSha</span><span class="p">);</span>
  <span class="kd">const</span> <span class="nx">cursor</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="k">new</span> <span class="nc">Cursor</span><span class="p">({</span> <span class="na">apiKey</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nx">process</span><span class="p">.</span><span class="nx">env</span><span class="p">.</span><span class="nx">CURSOR_API_KEY</span><span class="o">!</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="na">retry</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="kc">false</span> <span class="p">});</span>

    <span class="na">root</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nx">repoPath</span><span class="p">,</span>

  <span class="kd">const</span> <span class="na">suggestions</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nb">Record</span><span class="o">&lt;</span><span class="kr">string</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="kr">string</span><span class="p">[]</span><span class="o">&gt;</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="p">{};</span>

    <span class="kd">const</span> <span class="nx">key</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="s2">`</span><span class="p">${</span><span class="nx">msg</span><span class="p">.</span><span class="nx">repoId</span><span class="p">}</span><span class="s2">|</span><span class="p">${</span><span class="nx">msg</span><span class="p">.</span><span class="nx">filePath</span><span class="p">}</span><span class="s2">`</span><span class="p">;</span>
    <span class="k">if </span><span class="p">(</span><span class="o">!</span><span class="nx">suggestions</span><span class="p">[</span><span class="nx">key</span><span class="p">])</span> <span class="nx">suggestions</span><span class="p">[</span><span class="nx">key</span><span class="p">]</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="p">[];</span>
    <span class="nx">suggestions</span><span class="p">[</span><span class="nx">key</span><span class="p">].</span><span class="nf">push</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="nx">msg</span><span class="p">.</span><span class="nx">text</span><span class="p">);</span>
  <span class="p">});</span>

  <span class="c1">// -----------------------------------------------------------------</span>
  <span class="c1">// 4️⃣ For each changed file, ask Cursor for line‑by‑line suggestions.</span>
  <span class="c1">// -----------------------------------------------------------------</span>
  <span class="k">for </span><span class="p">(</span><span class="kd">const</span> <span class="nx">relPath</span> <span class="k">of</span> <span class="nx">changedFiles</span><span class="p">)</span> <span class="p">{</span>
    <span class="kd">const</span> <span class="nx">absPath</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="nf">join</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="nx">repoPath</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="nx">relPath</span><span class="p">);</span>
    <span class="kd">const</span> <span class="nx">fileContent</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="k">await</span> <span class="nx">fs</span><span class="p">.</span><span class="nf">readFile</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="nx">absPath</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="dl">"</span><span class="s2">utf-8</span><span class="dl">"</span><span class="p">);</span>

    <span class="c1">// Start listening *before* we send the request.</span>
    <span class="nf">startSuggestionStream</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="nx">repoId</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="nx">relPath</span><span class="p">);</span>

    <span class="c1">// Wrap the call so we can handle rate‑limit errors.</span>
    <span class="k">await</span> <span class="nf">safeSuggest</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="nx">cursor</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="p">{</span>
      <span class="nx">repoId</span><span class="p">,</span>
      <span class="na">filePath</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nx">relPath</span><span class="p">,</span>
      <span class="c1">// Provide the full content; Cursor will use the whole‑repo context internally.</span>
      <span class="na">content</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nx">fileContent</span><span class="p">,</span>
      <span class="c1">// Ask for a diff‑style suggestion.</span>
      <span class="na">mode</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="dl">"</span><span class="s2">diff</span><span class="dl">"</span><span class="p">,</span>
    <span class="p">});</span>
  <span class="p">}</span>

  <span class="c1">// -----------------------------------------------------------------</span>
  <span class="c1">// 5️⃣ Assemble a markdown comment with the collected diffs.</span>
  <span class="c1">// -----------------------------------------------------------------</span>
  <span class="kd">let</span> <span class="nx">commentBody</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="dl">"</span><span class="s2">### 🤖 Cursor AI suggestions</span><span class="se">\n\n</span><span class="dl">"</span><span class="p">;</span>

    <span class="kd">const</span> <span class="p">[,</span> <span class="nx">filePath</span><span class="p">]</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="nx">key</span><span class="p">.</span><span class="nf">split</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="dl">"</span><span class="s2">|</span><span class="dl">"</span><span class="p">);</span>

</blockquote>

<p><strong>Gotchas highlighted in the code</strong>  </p>

<ul>
<li>
<strong><code>require(esm)</code></strong> – Because we set <code>"type": "module"</code> the <code>import</code> statements work; if you forget this, Node will throw “Cannot use import statement outside a module.”
</li>
<li>
<strong>SnapStart + VPC</strong> – If you later attach a VPC to this Lambda, SnapStart (the pre‑warm optimization) won’t help because the cold‑start time is dominated by VPC ENI attachment, not by the JavaScript engine.
</li>
<li>
<strong>Provisioned Concurrency</strong> – Turning it on for a low‑traffic PR‑assistant can add $0.01 / hour per provisioned instance even when no PRs arrive. Monitor usage before enabling.
</li>
</ul>




<h2>
  
  
  The Takeaway
</h2>

<blockquote>
<p><strong>Key points you can act on today</strong>  </p>
</blockquote>

<ul>
<li>Whole‑repo context lets an LLM see cross‑file relationships, turning “autocomplete” into “architectural assistant.”
</li>
<li>Install the Cursor SDK as an ESM module, pin the version, and bundle <code>node_modules</code> to avoid the <code>require(esm)</code> pitfall.
</li>
<li>Use Node’s <code>diagnostics_channel</code> to receive suggestion chunks immediately, keeping the PR feedback loop fast.
</li>
<li>Turn off the SDK’s hidden retry logic; handle <code>CursorRateLimitError</code> yourself so Lambda timeouts stay predictable.
</li>
<li>A single Lambda can clone a repo, upload the entire tree, stream per‑file suggestions, and post a nicely formatted comment—all without a server.
</li>
</ul>

<p>With these steps you can move from treating Cursor as a fancy autocomplete to using it as a full‑context code reviewer that runs on demand, cost‑effectively, in a serverless environment. Happy coding!</p>

      <description><p>Every AI product reads a block of instructions before it ever sees your message. Who it is, what it refuses, how it formats answers, what it must never say. You do not write it and you are not shown it.</p>

<p>One repo has captured <strong>430 of them</strong>, organised by vendor. The leak angle is the boring part. Here is what is actually useful.</p>

<h2>
  
  
  The 13x gap
</h2>

<p>Anthropic <strong>publishes</strong> its Claude system prompts. Openly, on purpose, in the release notes. The repo stores those too, so you can put the published version next to the captured one.</p>

<p>They are not the same size:</p>

<ul>
<li>
<strong>Official, published by Anthropic:</strong> 4,269 words</li>
<li>
<strong>Captured from the running product:</strong> 56,148 words</li>
</ul>

<p>Roughly <strong>13 times larger</strong>.</p>

<p>That gap is not a scandal. Published prompts legitimately exclude tool definitions, per-surface instructions and operational scaffolding. But if you were studying the published version to learn how a frontier team writes prompts, you were reading a summary and did not know it.</p>

<p>Dropping both into a <a href="https://www.devpik.com/text-tools/text-diff" rel="noopener noreferrer">text diff</a> is the fastest way to see what the published version leaves out. That is the exercise I would actually recommend from this repo.</p>

<h2>
  
  
  What the prompts reveal
</h2>

<p>Read enough and patterns show up that no marketing page would state.</p>

<p><strong>Enormous effort goes into tone, not capability.</strong> Large fractions of every prompt are spent on how to <em>sound</em>. Do not open with flattery. Do not pad with caveats. Do not moralise. Vary sentence length. Providers clearly treat default LLM voice as a serious product problem and spend real prompt budget on it.</p>

<p><strong>Refusals are far more specific than public policy.</strong> Published safety policies are broad and principled. The prompts contain concrete enumerated categories. If a model ever refused something oddly specific, this is where that lives.</p>

<p>If you write system prompts for your own product, this is the closest thing to watching how the best-funded teams in the industry solve your exact problem. The formatting rules alone will improve your output.</p>

<h2>
  
  
  Stay sceptical
</h2>

<p>The repo says prompts are captured verbatim. Treat that carefully.</p>

<p>These are extracted by asking the model to repeat its instructions. It works because the prompt genuinely is in context and the model can read it back. But <strong>a model reproducing text from its context is not a guaranteed faithful copy.</strong> It can paraphrase, skip, smooth a section, or in the worst case confabulate something plausible.</p>

<p>Treat them as high quality evidence, not primary source documents. Patterns across many files are trustworthy. Any single exact sentence is less so.</p>

      <description><h2>
  
  
  Prompt Engineering: What’s New in September 2026
</h2>

<p>Based on my technical understanding as a Lead Programmer Analyst who has spent the last decade writing PHP, Perl, Python, and shell scripts for enterprise‑scale AI pipelines, I can say that the field of prompt engineering has finally crossed the “nice‑to‑have” threshold and entered the realm of production‑grade software development.  In September 2026 the landscape is no longer dominated by ad‑hoc temperature tweaks; it’s driven by structured reasoning effort, agentic workflows, and parallel‑agent orchestration.  This article walks you through the most consequential changes, the tools that are reshaping our daily work, and the concrete techniques you can start using right now.</p>

<h3>
  
  
  Table of Contents
</h3>

<ul>
<li>The New Prompt Parameter Landscape</li>
<li>Reasoning_Effort vs. Temperature</li>
<li>Claude 4.2 Agentic Workflows</li>

<li>Future Outlook</li>
<li>📚 References &amp; Further Reading</li>
<li>Your Turn</li>
</ul>

<h2>
  
  
  The New Prompt Parameter Landscape
</h2>

<p>Until early 2025, the dominant “knob” for most LLM APIs was <code>temperature</code>.  A lower value gave deterministic output; a higher value encouraged creativity.  In September 2026, the major providers—Anthropic (Claude Opus 5, Claude Sonnet 5), OpenAI (GPT‑5.6), and the emerging Cohere‑X series—have introduced a richer control surface:</p>

<p>ParameterProviderWhat It ControlsTypical Values</p>

<p><code>reasoning_effort</code>AnthropicHidden chain‑of‑thought token budget (Low/Medium/High)Low, Medium, High<br>
<code>creativity_factor</code>OpenAIPost‑hoc diversity after core reasoning is locked0‑2.0<br>
<code>parallelism_degree</code>OpenAINumber of concurrent reasoning threads (for GPT‑5.0 Parallel Agents)1‑8<br>
<code>agentic_mode</code>AnthropicEnables built‑in tool‑calling &amp; self‑reflection loopsauto / off</p>

<p>The shift is purposeful.  As the <a href="https://www.digitalapplied.com/blog/prompt-engineering-advanced-techniques-2026" rel="noopener noreferrer">Digital Applied article</a> notes, “the primary lever is no longer temperature—it’s <code>reasoning_effort</code> (Low/Medium/High), which controls hidden chain‑of‑thought tokens that drastically improve factual consistency.”  The practical upshot is that you can tell the model to spend more “thinking” budget on a request without sacrificing deterministic output, a capability that was impossible when temperature was the only dial.</p>
<h2>
  
  
  Reasoning_Effort vs. Temperature
</h2>

<p>Let’s unpack why <code>reasoning_effort</code> matters.  Under the hood, Anthropic’s Claude 5 series allocates a separate token pool for internal “thought” steps.  When you set <code>reasoning_effort=High</code>, the model inserts a hidden chain‑of‑thought (CoT) sequence that can be up to 2‑3× longer than the visible output.  These hidden tokens are never surfaced to the user but are used to:</p>

<ul>
<li>Perform self‑verification (e.g., “Check that the sum of X and Y matches Z”).</li>
<li>Generate fallback plans if the primary reasoning path fails a confidence check.</li>
<li>Cross‑reference internal knowledge graphs without exceeding the user‑visible token limit.</li>
</ul>

<p>In contrast, temperature only influences the probability distribution of the next token.  It does not allocate extra computation budget, so a high‑temperature request can still hallucinate because it never “thinks” deeply enough.</p>

## GPT‑5.0 Parallel Agents: Scaling Reasoning Across Cores

OpenAI’s GPT‑5.0 (currently at version 5.6) introduced `parallelism_degree`, which spins up multiple reasoning agents that work concurrently on sub‑tasks.  The result is a dramatic reduction in latency for complex, multi‑step problems such as code synthesis, data‑frame transformations, or multi‑modal reasoning.

How it works:

- The primary prompt is parsed into a *task graph* (similar to a DAG).
- Each node is assigned to a separate “agent” thread, respecting dependencies.
- Agents exchange hidden messages (internal CoT tokens) via a shared memory bus.
- When all nodes finish, the orchestrator merges the partial outputs into the final answer.

Below is a `curl` example that asks GPT‑5.6 to generate a full‑stack CRUD app, letting the model parallelize UI design, database schema, and API skeleton:

</code></pre>

python<br>

  -H "Authorization: Bearer $OPENAI_API_KEY" \<br>
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \<br>
  -d '{<br>
    "model": "gpt-5.6",<br>
    "prompt": "Create a minimal MERN stack app that tracks book loans. Include:<br>
      1. MongoDB schema<br>
      2. Express routes<br>
      3. React components for list, add, edit, delete<br>

    "max_tokens": 2048,<br>

    "parallelism_degree": 4,<br>

}'<br>

Parallel agents also open the door to **ensemble prompting**: you can ask three agents to solve the same sub‑task with different `reasoning_effort` levels and then let a meta‑agent vote on the best answer.  This pattern is already being used in high‑frequency trading firms to reduce model variance.

## Prompt Optimization Loops: GEPA and Execution‑Trace Mining

The [Techy Side guide](https://www.thetechyside.com.au/posts/a-practical-guide-to-prompt-engineering-in-september-2026) highlights a new research breakthrough called GEPA (Gradient‑Enhanced Prompt Augmentation).  Presented at ICLR 2026, GEPA treats the LLM’s execution trace as a differentiable graph, allowing you to back‑propagate a loss (e.g., “answer mismatch”) into the prompt text itself.

In practice, a GEPA loop looks like this:

- Generate an initial answer with a baseline prompt.
- Parse the hidden CoT trace (available via the `trace=true` flag on Claude 5 and GPT‑5.6).
- Compute a loss based on a downstream metric—such as SQL query correctness or unit‑test pass rate.
- Apply a small gradient step to the prompt tokens (treated as embeddings) and re‑render the prompt.
- Iterate until the loss plateaus.

Below is a minimal Python sketch using the `torch` autograd engine to perform a GEPA step on a Claude prompt.  The code assumes you have access to the internal `trace_embeddings` endpoint, which is currently in beta for enterprise customers.

</code></pre>

python</p>
<h1>

<p>import torch<br>
import anthropic</p>

      <title>Why Your AI Prompt Worked on Friday and Broke on Monday</title>
      <dc:creator>Peter</dc:creator>
      <pubDate>Wed, 16 Sep 2026 14:21:41 +0000</pubDate>
      <link>https://dev.to/trypromptflow/why-your-ai-prompt-worked-on-friday-and-broke-on-monday-184l</link>
      <guid>https://dev.to/trypromptflow/why-your-ai-prompt-worked-on-friday-and-broke-on-monday-184l</guid>
      <description><p>promptengineering# Why Your AI Prompt Worked on Friday and Broke on Monday</p>

<p>You wrote a prompt. You tested it. It worked. You deployed it on Friday afternoon, went home, came back on Monday, and the output is wrong.</p>

<p>Nothing changed in the prompt. Nobody touched the code. The same input goes in, but different output comes out. The formatting is off. Key fields are missing. The model that was producing clean, structured results on Friday is now returning something that looks like it came from a different system entirely.</p>

<p>This is one of the most frustrating failure modes in AI workflows, and it is also one of the most common. Teams spend hours tweaking the prompt, adding constraints, rewriting instructions, and chasing the new behavior. Sometimes the tweak works for a day or two. Then it breaks again. The cycle repeats.</p>

<p>The problem is almost never the prompt itself.</p>

<h2>
  
  
  The Visible Issue vs. The Root Issue
</h2>

<p>The visible issue is that the output changed. The root issue is that something in the environment around the prompt shifted over the weekend. The data, the context, the model, or the expectations. The prompt was written for a specific set of conditions, and those conditions no longer hold.</p>

<p>When you tweak the prompt to chase the new behavior, you are patching a symptom. The underlying drift continues, and the next Monday you are back where you started, rewriting instructions that worked fine three days ago.</p>

<h2>
  
  
  Four Causes of Weekend Degradation
</h2>

<p>Four categories cover most cases where a prompt was fine on Friday and broken by Monday. Understanding which one applies is the difference between a 15-minute fix and a two-hour guessing game.</p>

<h3>
  
  
  1. Input Drift
</h3>

<p>The data feeding into the prompt changed over the weekend. New records were added to a database, a source system pushed a schema update, or an upstream pipeline modified the shape of the data. The prompt still fires, but it is operating on inputs it was not designed for.</p>

<p>Example: A summarization prompt expects article bodies as plain text. Over the weekend, the content management system was updated to include HTML markup in the body field. The prompt now receives <code>&lt;p&gt;</code> tags and <code>&lt;div&gt;</code> wrappers mixed into the text. The model tries to process it, but the markup confuses the structure. The summary comes out fragmented.</p>

<p>The prompt did not fail. The input contract changed.</p>

<h3>
  
  
  2. Expectation Drift
</h3>

<p>The team's definition of "good output" shifted. A stakeholder reviewed results over the weekend and decided the format, tone, or structure needs to change. The prompt still produces exactly what it always produced, but that is no longer what anyone wants.</p>

<p>Example: A report-generation prompt was producing summaries in paragraph form. Over the weekend, a director decided they want bullet points instead. Nobody updated the prompt. Nobody told the engineer. The prompt runs Monday morning, produces paragraphs, and gets flagged as "broken" because the expectations moved while the prompt stayed still.</p>

<p>This is the hardest one to diagnose because technically nothing is wrong. The prompt is doing exactly what it was told to do. The gap is between what the prompt produces and what the team now expects.</p>

<h3>
  
  
  3. Context-Window Pressure
</h3>

<p>The prompt worked when context was lean. Over the weekend, accumulated context (conversation history, retrieved documents, prior outputs) pushed the effective input past a threshold. The model starts dropping or summarizing earlier instructions, and the output degrades.</p>

<p>Example: A customer support prompt includes the system instructions, a knowledge base retrieval, and the last 10 messages in the conversation. On Friday, the knowledge base returned 3 documents totaling 2,000 tokens. Over the weekend, new articles were published, and the retrieval now returns 8 documents totaling 6,000 tokens. The system instructions that were comfortably within the context window on Friday are now being truncated or deprioritized. The model starts ignoring formatting rules that lived in the system prompt.</p>

<p>The prompt is unchanged. The context budget is consumed by something else.</p>

<h3>
  
  
  4. Model Behavior Drift
</h3>

<p>The underlying model was updated or reconfigured. Providers push changes quietly, and the same prompt can produce measurably different output after a model revision. The prompt is unchanged, but the engine interpreting it is not.</p>

<p>Example: A prompt was tuned for a specific model version. The provider rolled out an update over the weekend that changed how the model handles structured output. JSON formatting that was reliable on Friday now includes markdown code fences around the JSON. Downstream parsing breaks.</p>

<p>You cannot control this. But you can detect it. If the prompt, the input, and the expectations are all unchanged, model behavior drift is the likely culprit.</p>

<h2>
  
  
  A Real-World Example
</h2>

<p>Consider a sales ops team that uses a prompt to summarize the week's pipeline activity every Monday morning. The prompt pulls from the CRM, formats deals into a summary table, and highlights risks.</p>

<p>On Friday afternoon, it worked perfectly. Clean tables, accurate risk flags, ready for the leadership meeting.</p>

<p>On Monday, the summary is a mess. Tables are misaligned, risk flags are missing, and the output requires manual cleanup before it is usable. The team assumes the prompt is broken and spends two hours tweaking formatting instructions.</p>

<p>What actually happened: Over the weekend, the CRM pushed a schema update that added two new fields to the deal records. The prompt was not written to handle them, so the model improvised. The formatting broke as a result.</p>

<p>The prompt did not fail. The input contract changed, and the prompt had no guardrails for that scenario. The fix was not another formatting instruction. The fix was recognizing that the prompt depended on a specific input structure that was never documented, never tested, and never protected.</p>

<h2>
  
  
  Diagnostic Reframing
</h2>

<p>Instead of asking "what is wrong with the prompt," ask four questions:</p>

<p><strong>What changed between Friday and Monday?</strong> Look at inputs, model versions, context size, and any stakeholder feedback that arrived over the weekend. This is your starting point. If you cannot identify what changed, you cannot diagnose the failure.</p>

<p><strong>What does the prompt assume?</strong> List every implicit assumption the prompt makes: about input format, data availability, context length, and expected output shape. These are the assumptions that break silently. A prompt that says "summarize the following article" assumes the input is a single article in plain text. If either assumption breaks, the output degrades.</p>

<p><strong>Where is the drift?</strong> Map each assumption to what actually changed. The intersection is your root cause. If the prompt assumes plain text input and the input now contains HTML, that is your drift. If the prompt assumes 3,000 tokens of context and the retrieval now returns 8,000, that is your drift.</p>

<p><strong>What guardrail would prevent this next time?</strong> A guardrail might be an input validation step that checks the input format before it reaches the prompt. It might be a context-length check that logs a warning when retrieval exceeds a threshold. It might be a model-version pin that prevents silent updates. Or it might be an output contract that fails loudly instead of degrading quietly.</p>

<p>This reframing moves the conversation from "fix the words" to "fix the system." The prompt is one component. The environment around it is the rest.</p>

<h2>
  
  
  Common Patterns
</h2>

<p>After diagnosing enough weekend-breakage incidents, the same patterns repeat:</p>

<p><strong>Pattern 1: The silent schema change.</strong> An upstream system updates its data format. Nobody tells the prompt owner. The prompt processes the new format and produces degraded output. The team blames the prompt. The actual fix is adding an input validation layer that detects schema changes before they reach the model.</p>

<p><strong>Pattern 2: The context creep.</strong> A retrieval system was configured with a certain document count. Over time, more documents get indexed. The retrieval returns more context than the prompt was designed for. The model starts ignoring earlier instructions. The fix is a context budget that caps the total tokens fed to the model and logs when the cap is hit.</p>

<p><strong>Pattern 3: The expectation whiplash.</strong> A stakeholder changes what they want the output to look like. The prompt keeps producing the old format. The team treats this as a bug when it is actually a requirements change. The fix is a documented output spec that gets versioned alongside the prompt.</p>

<p><strong>Pattern 4: The invisible model update.</strong> The provider pushes a model update. The same prompt produces different output. There is no changelog, no notification, no version bump you can point to. The fix is a regression test suite that runs the prompt against a fixed set of inputs and compares the output structure (not the exact text) against a baseline.</p>

<h2>
  
  
  When to Run This Diagnostic
</h2>

<p>Run this diagnostic any time a prompt that was working starts producing different output without a code change. Specifically:</p>

<ul>
<li>
<strong>Monday mornings</strong>, if the prompt runs on a schedule and the output looks different from Friday</li>
<li>
<strong>After upstream system updates</strong>, even if the update seems unrelated to the prompt</li>
<li>
<strong>After model provider announcements</strong>, even if the announcement says "no breaking changes"</li>
<li>
<strong>After team feedback sessions</strong>, where expectations may have shifted</li>
</ul>

<p>The faster you run the diagnostic, the faster you find the root cause. The longer you wait, the more changes accumulate, and the harder it becomes to isolate which one caused the breakage.</p>

<h2>
  
  
  Building Habits
</h2>

<p>The teams that handle this well have one thing in common: they treat prompts as software, not as static documents. That means:</p>

<ul>
<li>Version your prompts the same way you version code</li>
<li>Document the assumptions each prompt makes about its inputs</li>
<li>Write output contracts that define what "correct" looks like</li>
<li>Run regression tests against a fixed input set on a schedule</li>
<li>Log the context size and input format on every run, so you can compare when things break</li>
</ul>

<p>None of this requires fancy tooling. It requires the discipline to treat the prompt as part of a system, not as a standalone artifact. The prompt is one component. The inputs, the context, the model, and the expectations are the rest. When the output breaks, check all of them.</p>
